cna.title: vm2: GHSA-8hg8-63c5-gwmx patch bypass: nesting:true without explicit require still allows full RCE

descriptions.value: vm2 is an open source vm/sandbox for Node.js. Prior to version 3.11.4, the fix for GHSA-8hg8-63c5-gwmx (CVE-2023-37903) introduced a check in nodevm.js line 263 that blocks the combination nesting: true + require: false. However, the check uses strict equality (options.require === false), which is trivially bypassed by omitting the require option entirely. When require is not specified, options.require is undefined, not false. The strict equality check fails, so the security guard is skipped. Immediately after (line 280), the destructuring default require: requireOpts = false assigns requireOpts = false, producing the exact configuration the patch was designed to prevent. This issue has been patched in version 3.11.4.

cna.title: pam_usb: OTP pad authentication bypass via missing system pad check and uninitialized RNG buffer

descriptions.value: pam_usb provides hardware authentication for Linux using ordinary removable media. Prior to 0.9.0, the pusb_pad_compare() function in src/pad.c only verified that the user-side pad (~/.pamusb/device.pad) could be read, but did not enforce that the system-side pad (the pad file on the USB device) was also present and readable. If the user-side pad was deleted or unreadable, the function returned a failure that was treated as non-fatal in certain code paths, allowing authentication to succeed without the USB device being verified. A local user can delete their own ~/.pamusb/device.pad to remove the USB device requirement and authenticate without the physical device. This vulnerability is fixed in 0.9.0.

cna.title: PraisonAI Platform has a cross-workspace IDOR + member-role privilege escalation

descriptions.value: PraisonAI Platform is the platform layer for the PraisonAI multi-agent teams system. Prior to version 0.1.4, the Platform server exposes resources under `/api/v1/workspaces/{workspace_id}/...` and protects them with a `require_workspace_member(workspace_id)` FastAPI dependency. The dependency only checks that the caller is a member of the workspace_id in the URL prefix. The route handlers then look up the inner resource (`agent_id`, `issue_id`, `project_id`, `label_id`, `comment_id`, `dependency_id`) by primary key alone. The resource's own `workspace_id` is never compared to the URL's `workspace_id`. A user can therefore put their own workspace in the URL prefix and any other workspace's resource ID in the path. The auth check passes, since they really are a member of the prefix workspace. The service then returns the cross-tenant resource for read, update, or delete. There is a second bug in the member-management routes (`add_member`, `update_member_role`, `remove_member`, `update_workspace`, `delete_workspace`). Each one inherits the default `min_role="member"` from `require_workspace_member`. Any basic member can therefore promote themselves to admin or owner, demote or remove other members, and delete the workspace. The role hierarchy exists in the schema but is not enforced. Registration is open at `/api/v1/auth/register` with no email verification. The default server bind is `0.0.0.0:8000` (`python -m praisonai_platform`). One curl from any unauthenticated network position is enough to bootstrap into the system. PraisonAI Platform version 0.1.4 patches the issue.

cna.title: Net::IMAP: Command Injection via non-synchronizing literal in "raw" argument

descriptions.value: Net::IMAP implements Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) client functionality in Ruby. Prior to 0.6.5 and 0.5.15, several Net::IMAP commands accept a "raw data" argument that is sent verbatim after validation to prevent command injection. However, if a server does not support non-synchronizing literals, it may still be possible to inject arbitrary IMAP commands inside non-synchronizing literals.  A server without support for non-synchronizing literals may interpret the "+}\r\n" as the end of a malformed command line and respond with a tagged BAD. In that case, the contents of the literal will be interpreted as one or more new pipelined commands, allowing a CRLF command injection attack to succeed. This affects criteria for #search and #uid_search; search_keys for #sort, #thread, #uid_sort, and #uid_thread; and attr for #fetch and #uid_fetch. This vulnerability is fixed in 0.6.5 and 0.5.15.

@fastify/middie is the middleware engine that adds Express and Connect style middleware support to Fastify. In versions up to and including 9.3.6, middie builds the match regular expression for each path-scoped middleware from its mount path without collapsing duplicate slashes, even when the application enables the ignoreDuplicateSlashes router option. Under that option Fastify's router collapses duplicate slashes in both the registered route and the request path, so a mount path containing a doubled slash is served by the router at its single-slash form while the middleware's compiled match still requires the doubled slash and never matches. A path-scoped middleware such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting is therefore skipped while the router dispatches the request to the protected handler, without any authentication required. Applications are affected when they enable ignoreDuplicateSlashes and a middleware mount path reaches middie with a duplicate slash, most commonly when a plugin prefix that ends with a slash is joined to a mount path that starts with one. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.7, and users should upgrade to 9.3.7 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, and avoid mount paths and plugin prefixes that introduce duplicate slashes.

x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix removes the sync-permission exception from the authorization check in captureSGExisting. The condition is simplified to unconditionally require that the user passes checkIfAuthorised for the target sharing group, regardless of whether the user holds the sync role. This ensures sync users are subject to the same membership verification as all other users before a sharing group can be modified.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; the vulnerability is assumed to affect all versions containing the flawed captureSGExisting logic prior to this commit.

The CVSS SC:H rating assumes that the events in a non-member sharing group contain sensitive threat intelligence data whose disclosure constitutes a high confidentiality impact; if the data is less sensitive, SC could be rated L.

The CAPEC-114 mapping is the closest standard pattern; the specific mechanism is a logic flaw in an authorization condition rather than a classic privilege escalation, but CAPEC-114 (Bypass Authorization) is the best available match.
The sync role (perm_sync) is assumed to be a standard MISP role for inter-instance synchronization; the exact role configuration is not detailed in the patch.
The Co-Authored-By line references an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5); this is not included as a credit as it is not a human or organizational entity in the traditional CVE credit sense.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/SharingGroup.php, the captureSGExisting method's guard clause was changed from 'if (!checkIfAuthorised(...) && !perm_sync) return false' to 'if (!checkIfAuthorised(...)) return false'. The '&& !$user[Role][perm_sync]' clause was removed, eliminating the bypass that allowed sync-role users to skip the membership authorization check. One line changed (1 insertion, 1 deletion).
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N - MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L - exploitation requires only a valid sync account and a known sharing group UUID; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N - no attack target manipulation. PR:L - requires an authenticated account with the sync role. UI:N - no victim interaction needed. VC:N/VI:N/VA:N - the MISP system's own operational integrity and availability are not directly compromised. SC:H - the primary impact is unauthorized read access to threat intelligence events belonging to other organisations (subsequent component confidentiality). SI:L - the attacker can modify the sharing group record (add org or all_orgs entry), a limited integrity impact on shared data. SA:N - no security authority impact.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker leverages a legitimate role (sync) that was incorrectly coded to bypass the authorization check, gaining access to resources (sharing group events) they are not entitled to. This is a direct authorization bypass. The mapping is confident because the patch explicitly removes a condition that allowed a specific role to skip the authorization check.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The authorization check (checkIfAuthorised) was effectively bypassed for users with the sync role due to a flawed logical condition. The membership verification was not enforced for sync users, constituting a missing authorization control for that user class.

The authorization logic incorrectly combined the membership check with a role-based exemption using a logical AND, resulting in an improper authorization decision that permitted sync users to act outside their granted scope.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-114 Bypass Authorization

solutions.value: The fix removes the sync-permission exception from the authorization check in captureSGExisting. The condition is simplified to unconditionally require that the user passes checkIfAuthorised for the target sharing group, regardless of whether the user holds the sync role. This ensures sync users are subject to the same membership verification as all other users before a sharing group can be modified.

descriptions.value:
MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform) contains an authorization bypass in the SharingGroup model's captureSGExisting method. The authorization check used a logical AND condition that effectively exempted users with the sync permission (perm_sync) from the membership verification. Specifically, the original condition 'if (!checkIfAuthorised(...) && !perm_sync) return false' meant that any user holding the sync role would pass the check regardless of whether they were actually a member of the target sharing group.

A sync user who knows or can discover the UUID of a non-local sharing group could exploit this flaw through the /sharing_groups/add endpoint or by embedding a SharingGroup object in pushed sync data. The attacker could rewrite the sharing group record to add their own organisation as a member or insert an all_orgs server entry for their MISP instance, thereby gaining read access to all events contained in that group. This exposes threat intelligence data that was intended to be restricted to the group's legitimate members.

The vulnerability requires an authenticated account with the sync role and knowledge of a valid sharing group UUID. No user interaction is required. The impact is unauthorized disclosure of shared threat intelligence events and limited integrity modification of the sharing group record.

x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The tag endpoints now load their target event or attribute using ACL-aware fetch methods (fetchSimpleEvent, fetchAttributeSimple) that apply the calling user's visibility rules before returning the object. A hidden event or attribute now produces the same response as a non-existent one, eliminating both the tag-enumeration information leak and the ability of host-organisation users to modify tags on records they cannot see. A clarifying comment was added to ACLComponent::canModifyTag to document that the caller must load the object with visibility applied first.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; all versions prior to this commit are assumed affected.
PR:L assumes the attacker needs only the tagger role (perm_tagger) or host-org membership, which is a low-privilege role in MISP's model; the exact minimum role was inferred from the test setup.
VC:L assumes the tag-enumeration information disclosure is a low confidentiality impact; if the tag names themselves are considered sensitive, the impact could be higher.

CAPEC-128 was selected as the closest match; CAPEC-100 (Parameter Tampering) is a secondary candidate but the root cause is server-side missing visibility scoping rather than client-side parameter manipulation.
The commit date (2026-11-10) and the presence of 'Claude Opus 5.5' as co-author are taken at face value from the patch metadata; no independent verification was performed.

x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In EventsController::addTag (single and bulk paths) and EventsController::removeTag, replaced unscoped $this->Event->find('first', ['recursive' => -1, ...]) calls with $this->Event->fetchSimpleEvent($this->Auth->user(), $id), and added an explicit empty-check in removeTag returning 'Invalid event.' for hidden targets. In AttributesController::removeTag, replaced $this->MispAttribute->find('first', ['recursive' => -1, ...]) with $this->MispAttribute->fetchAttributeSimple($this->Auth->user(), [...]). Added a documentation comment in ACLComponent::canModifyTag noting that the event or attribute must be loaded with the user's visibility applied before the check. Added a regression test class TagEndpointsHiddenTargets covering hidden-event tag enumeration, host-org tag add/remove on hidden and visible records, bulk addTag, and site-admin behaviour.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a web application accessed over the network. AC:L: The attack requires only a standard API call with a known or guessable event/attribute ID; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is needed. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated user with at least the tagger role (perm_tagger) or host-organisation membership; this is a low-privilege requirement in MISP's role model. UI:N: No user interaction is required. VC:L: The removeTag endpoint leaks which tags are present on a hidden event, a limited confidentiality impact on metadata. VI:L: Host-org users can add or remove local tags on hidden events/attributes, a limited integrity impact on tag metadata. VA:N: No availability impact. capecRationale.rationale: MISP implements a custom ACL/visibility system for events and attributes. The tag endpoints incorrectly implemented this access control by loading the target object without applying the user's visibility filter before performing the operation. The access control mechanism existed (canModifyTag) but was applied to an unscoped object, making it ineffective. This is the closest CAPEC to the observed pattern of a custom authorization check being bypassed due to incorrect implementation. Uncertainty: CAPEC-100 (Parameter Tampering) could also apply since the attacker supplies an ID of a record they cannot see, but the root cause is the missing visibility scoping in the server-side load, making CAPEC-128 the more precise match.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The tag endpoints performed tag add/remove operations on events and attributes without first verifying that the calling user had visibility (ACL) on the target object. The authorization check (canModifyTag) was applied to an unscoped object, effectively missing the visibility authorization step.
The removeTag endpoint returned different responses for a tag present versus absent on a hidden event, leaking information about the tag set of records the user was not authorized to view.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-128 Exploiting Incorrectly Implemented Custom Access Control

solutions.value: The tag endpoints now load their target event or attribute using ACL-aware fetch methods (fetchSimpleEvent, fetchAttributeSimple) that apply the calling user's visibility rules before returning the object. A hidden event or attribute now produces the same response as a non-existent one, eliminating both the tag-enumeration information leak and the ability of host-organisation users to modify tags on records they cannot see. A clarifying comment was added to ACLComponent::canModifyTag to document that the caller must load the object with visibility applied first.

descriptions.value: MISP contains an access control flaw in its tag management endpoints: events/addTag (single and bulk), events/removeTag, and attributes/removeTag. These endpoints loaded their target event or attribute using an unscoped database query (recursive = -1) that did not apply the calling user's ACL visibility rules. As a result, two distinct security issues existed: (1) Information disclosure: the removeTag endpoint returned different responses depending on whether a given tag was present on a hidden event, allowing an authenticated user to enumerate which tags were applied to events they had no visibility into. (2) Unauthorized modification: users belonging to the host organisation, who are permitted to set local tags on records they can see, could add or remove local tags on events and attributes they could not see, because the canModifyTag ACL check operated on the unscoped object without first verifying the caller's visibility. The fix replaces the unscoped find() calls with ACL-aware fetch methods (fetchSimpleEvent and fetchAttributeSimple) that apply the user's visibility before the object is returned, and adds an explicit empty-object check in removeTag so that a hidden event responds identically to a non-existent one. Affected components include the EventsController (addTag, removeTag), the AttributesController (removeTag), and the ACLComponent (canModifyTag). The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with at least the tagger role (perm_tagger) or host-organisation membership.

workarounds.value:
On systems where a graphical login interface is not required (such as headless servers), disable the GDM service and configure the system to boot into multi-user target mode:

systemctl set-default multi-user.target
systemctl stop gdm.service

Warning: Stopping gdm.service immediately terminates any active graphical desktop sessions. Systems remain accessible via SSH and text-based virtual consoles. For systems requiring a graphical desktop environment, no supported configuration workaround exists to disable this interface without impacting display manager functionality.

x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix adds an event-level authorization check in the controller using fetchSimpleEvent, which enforces the user's distribution and sharing-group permissions and returns a uniform 404 for both hidden and non-existent events. The Default correlation engine now applies ACL conditions (organisation, event/attribute/object distribution, sharing-group membership) to the queried event's own attributes in both the correlation collection query and the related-events query. The OnDemand engine now includes the source attribute ID in its post-query ACL filter so that correlations are discarded if either side of the row is invisible to the user.
assumptions: The affected version range is unknown; the patch does not specify a version boundary. All MISP releases prior to this commit are assumed affected.

PR:L assumes that any authenticated user with the least-privileged role (perm_add) can trigger the vulnerability, as demonstrated by the regression tests. If a higher privilege level is required in some deployments, PR would be H.

VC:L assumes the exposed data (attribute values such as IPs and domains) constitutes a partial but not total loss of confidentiality. If the deployment treats all attribute data as highly sensitive, VC could be argued as H.

CAPEC-114 (Parameter Tampering) is selected as the closest match; CAPEC-126 (Leveraging Trusted Relationships) is an alternative but less precise mapping for the missing per-resource authorization check.
The commit date (2026-11-09) is taken at face value from the patch metadata; no independent verification of the timeline is performed.
The Co-Authored-By line credits Claude Opus 5.5 as a remediation developer; this is recorded as metadata evidence without independent verification of the contribution.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: CorrelationsController.php: added a fetchSimpleEvent call before processing; throws NotFoundException if the event is not visible to the user, and casts the resolved ID to int. DefaultCorrelationBehavior.php: added a new __aclConditions() private method that builds SQL OR/AND conditions for org_id, event_distribution, event_sharing_group_id, object_distribution, object_sharing_group_id, distribution, and sharing_group_id; these conditions are merged into the __collectCorrelations query and the __filterRelatedEvents query. OnDemandCorrelationBehavior.php: __filterCorrelationsByAcl now collects both the target attribute ID and the source_id into the ACL check set, and the visibility test requires both to be present. tests/testregressions.py: added EventCorrelationsAcl test class with four test methods covering invisible-event 404, hidden-attribute filtering, related-event filtering, and owner/admin regression.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L: exploitation requires only a valid session and a target event ID; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N: no attack-target manipulation is needed. PR:L: any authenticated user with the least-privileged role can trigger the issue; no admin or specific role required. UI:N: no victim interaction needed. VC:L: partial confidentiality loss - attribute IDs and values (IPs, domains) of hidden events/attributes are disclosed, but not full database or credential exposure. VI:N, VA:N: no integrity or availability impact. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: no impact beyond the vulnerable component itself.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker manipulates the event ID path parameter in the correlations/eventCorrelations/<id> endpoint to reference an event they are not authorised to view. The server accepted the parameter without validating the caller's access to that specific event. This is the closest CAPEC to the observed attack: the user supplies a parameter value (event ID) that the application fails to authorize. Uncertainty: CAPEC-126 (Leveraging Trusted Relationships) is also plausible because the user leverages a valid session, but the core defect is the missing per-resource authorization check triggered by the tampered parameter.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The eventCorrelations action performed no check that the authenticated user was permitted to view the event identified by the event ID parameter before returning its correlations. This is a classic missing authorization check at the resource level.

The correlation engines applied ACL filtering only to the target (related) side of each correlation row and omitted the queried event's own source attributes. This is an incomplete/incorrect authorization check that allowed hidden attribute data to be exposed.

solutions.value: The fix adds an event-level authorization check in the controller using fetchSimpleEvent, which enforces the user's distribution and sharing-group permissions and returns a uniform 404 for both hidden and non-existent events. The Default correlation engine now applies ACL conditions (organisation, event/attribute/object distribution, sharing-group membership) to the queried event's own attributes in both the correlation collection query and the related-events query. The OnDemand engine now includes the source attribute ID in its post-query ACL filter so that correlations are discarded if either side of the row is invisible to the user.

descriptions.value: MISP contains an authorization bypass in the correlations/eventCorrelations endpoint and the underlying correlation engines (Default and OnDemand). The CorrelationsController::eventCorrelations action did not verify that the requesting user was permitted to view the event specified by the event ID parameter. Any authenticated user could supply the ID of an event belonging to another organisation (distribution level 0, organisation-only) and receive its full correlation results, including attribute identifiers and values. Additionally, for events the user could partially view, the correlation engines filtered only the related (target) side of each correlation row and did not vet the queried event's own source attributes. As a result, correlations keyed by attributes hidden from the user (organisation-only attributes, attributes in sharing groups the user is not a member of, or attributes inside organisation-only objects) were returned with their IDs and values. The Default engine's related-event listing (used in events/view) also included events related solely through such hidden attributes. The vulnerability was reported by ENISA. Successful exploitation requires a valid authenticated session with any role and knowledge or enumeration of a target event ID. The security impact is disclosure of threat-intelligence attribute values (IP addresses, domain names, etc.) and attribute identifiers that the user is not authorised to see, as well as confirmation of the existence of otherwise invisible events.

cna.title: Librelp: certificate validation bypass in certvalid tls authentication mode

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank s4cr00t (Alipay Security Team) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
Restrict network reachability to the RELP service port using firewall rules so that only authorized systems can establish connections, or switch to an alternate authentication mode such as "fingerprint" or "name".

To restrict the RELP port (default 20514/tcp) to authorized IP addresses using firewalld:

firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=<TRUSTED_IP_OR_SUBNET>
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-port=20514/tcp
firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-port=20514/tcp
firewall-cmd --reload

Alternatively, if RELP network logging is not essential, disable the imrelp or omrelp configuration in /etc/rsyslog.conf or /etc/rsyslog.d/ and restart rsyslog:

systemctl restart rsyslog

Caveats:
Restricting access via firewall rules prevents connections from untrusted networks but does not prevent spoofing from hosts residing within the trusted IP range. Disabling RELP modules or changing authentication modes prevents log forwarding until all participating systems are reconfigured.

Warning: Modifying firewall configurations requires reloading firewalld, and changing rsyslog settings requires restarting the rsyslog daemon, which will cause a brief interruption in log handling.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in librelp. When configured to use Transport Layer Security (TLS) with certificate validation and the GnuTLS driver, the library fails to verify the peer certificate chain. @fastify/middie is the middleware engine that adds Express and Connect style middleware support to Fastify. In versions up to and including 9.3.6, middie does not honor the router's caseSensitive setting and matches path-scoped middleware mount paths with a case-insensitive regular expression that does not fold non-ASCII characters, while Fastify's router, when caseSensitive is set to false, lowercases the request path with a Unicode-aware conversion that maps the KELVIN SIGN character (U+212A) to the ASCII letter k. A request that spells a k in a protected mount path as the percent-encoded KELVIN SIGN is therefore routed to the protected handler while the middleware mounted on that path, such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting, never matches and is skipped, letting an unauthenticated client reach the handler. Only applications that set caseSensitive to false and protect a mount path containing the letter k are affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.7, and users should upgrade to 9.3.7 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, or keep routing case-sensitive, which is the default.

cna.title: Concurrent formatted-number parsing can return another caller's value

descriptions.value: CAPEC-26 Leveraging Race Conditions

In Eclipse Yasson versions 3.0 to 3.0.5, a race condition (CWE-362) exists in the handling of @JsonbNumberFormat. Yasson creates one java.text.NumberFormat instance per annotated property and shares it across all threads that use the same Jsonb instance. NumberFormat is not thread-safe, and the deserializer called parse() on it without synchronization. When multiple threads deserialize concurrently, a thread can receive a numeric value that belongs to another thread's input, receive an incorrect value, or fail with an exception. A remote attacker who can send concurrent requests to an application that deserializes untrusted JSON this way may cause incorrect data to be processed or cause another user's value to be returned. Exploitation requires that the application use @JsonbNumberFormat with a shared Jsonb instance and that the attacker win a timing race. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.6 by synchronizing access to the shared NumberFormat instances.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Galaxy cluster imports no longer take over

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Galaxy cluster imports no longer take over
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix adds an authorization check (__mayUpdateCapturedCluster) before any update to an existing Galaxy Cluster, permitting the operation only for the cluster's owner organization, a sync user with visibility to the cluster, or a site administrator. It also introduces a CAPTURE_FIELDS allow-list applied via CakePHP's fieldList option on save(), which restricts writable fields and explicitly excludes org_id and orgc_id from the update path, preventing ownership transfer. The captureOrganisationAndSG() call is moved after the authorization check so that a rejected request cannot alter ownership.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; the vulnerability is assumed to affect all versions containing the pre-fix captureCluster() implementation.
The galaxy editor role (perm_galaxy_editor) is assumed to be a non-administrative, non-trivial permission that can be granted to multiple organizations on a shared MISP instance.

CVSS VC is rated None because the primary demonstrated impact is integrity (modification and ownership transfer); any incidental confidentiality exposure via error messages is not the core vulnerability.

CAPEC-114 (Parameter Tampering) is the closest available mapping; the core flaw is missing authorization rather than parameter manipulation per se, but no CAPEC more precisely describes 'using a valid resource identifier to perform an unauthorized operation.'

The 'default' field exclusion from CAPTURE_FIELDS is noted in the commit message but its specific security significance is not further detailed in the patch; it is assumed to prevent modification of a cluster's default/flag status.
The Co-Authored-By line references an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5); it is credited as a tool rather than a human remediation developer.
No specific MISP release version is identified as the first fixed version; the commit date (2026-11-10) is the only temporal anchor available.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/GalaxyCluster.php: (1) Added a private const CAPTURE_FIELDS array listing the only fields captureCluster() may write, excluding the 'default' field. (2) Moved the existingGalaxyCluster lookup and the locked-cluster check before the captureOrganisationAndSG() call. (3) Added a call to the new __mayUpdateCapturedCluster() method that enforces owner-org, sync-user-visibility, or site-admin authorization. (4) Changed both save() calls to use ['fieldList' => self::CAPTURE_FIELDS]; the update path further removes org_id and orgc_id from the field list. (5) Added the __mayUpdateCapturedCluster() private method implementing the three-way authorization check. In tests/testregressions.py: added a GalaxyClusterCaptureUpdateGate test class with six test cases covering cross-org refusal, owner acceptance, sync-user visibility gating, and ownership preservation.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application; the import endpoint is reachable over HTTP. AC:L: The attacker needs only a valid galaxy-editor account and a target cluster UUID (discoverable via API enumeration or prior knowledge); no race condition or special timing is required. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is needed. PR:L: The attacker requires an authenticated account with the perm_galaxy_editor role, which is a non-trivial but not administrative privilege. UI:N: No victim interaction is required; the import is a server-side API call. VC:N: The primary impact is on integrity of cluster data and ownership; while an attacker could read cluster fields in error responses, the vulnerability is not a confidentiality bypass. VI:H: The attacker can overwrite cluster content (value, description, distribution, etc.) and transfer ownership (org_id, orgc_id) of clusters belonging to other organizations, severely compromising data integrity. VA:N: No denial-of-service impact is evident. SC:N: No impact on connected or downstream systems is demonstrated. SI:H: The integrity of shared threat-intelligence data across the MISP instance is compromised, affecting all consumers of the affected clusters. SA:N: No impact on the security posture of other systems.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker manipulates the UUID parameter in the galaxies/import request to target a specific Galaxy Cluster belonging to another organization. The system uses this user-supplied identifier to locate and overwrite the target row without validating the caller's authorization over that resource. This is the closest CAPEC to the observed attack: a legitimate API parameter (UUID) is used to redirect the operation to an unauthorized target. Uncertainty: CAPEC-114 typically describes tampering with multiple parameters or injecting unexpected values; here the parameter value is a valid UUID, and the core flaw is the missing authorization check rather than the parameter itself. However, no CAPEC more precisely captures 'using a valid resource identifier to perform an unauthorized operation on that resource,' making CAPEC-114 the best available match.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The captureCluster() update path performed no check that the requesting user was authorized to modify the specific cluster identified by UUID. Any user with the galaxy editor role could update and take ownership of clusters belonging to other organizations. The authorization logic was entirely absent for the cross-organization case.

The cluster UUID, supplied by the attacker in the import payload, was used as the sole key to identify the target row for update without verifying that the caller had a legitimate relationship (ownership, sharing-group visibility, or admin role) to that specific resource.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an authorization flaw in the GalaxyCluster model's captureCluster() function, which handles the import and synchronization of Galaxy Clusters. Prior to the fix, any authenticated user holding the galaxy editor role could replace an existing locked Galaxy Cluster by supplying its UUID in an import request, regardless of which organization owned the cluster. The function unconditionally called captureOrganisationAndSG() before the save operation, overwriting the cluster's org_id and orgc_id fields with the importing user's organization, effectively transferring ownership of the cluster to the attacker's organization. Additionally, the save operation was not restricted to a specific set of fields, allowing arbitrary field modification.

The vulnerable behavior required the attacker to possess a valid MISP account with the perm_galaxy_editor role and to know or discover the UUID of a target cluster belonging to another organization. No site-admin or owner-organization privilege was enforced for the update path. The result was that a low-privilege galaxy editor in one organization could modify the content (value, description, distribution, etc.) of clusters owned by other organizations and seize ownership, corrupting the integrity of shared threat-intelligence data across the MISP instance.

The vulnerability was reported by ENISA and CERT.pl. The fix introduces an explicit authorization gate that restricts cluster updates to the owner organization, a sync user who can see the cluster via sharing-group rules, or a site administrator, and enforces a field allow-list that excludes org_id and orgc_id from update writes, preserving original ownership.

cna.title: Rapid7 Metasploit Framework Local Privilege Escalation via Insecure msfdb PostgreSQL Configuration

descriptions.value:
Rapid7 Metasploit Framework versions prior to 6.5.10 suffer from an Improper Access Control issue in the msfdb database initialisation component whereby a PostgreSQL cluster initialised via msfdb init is configured with trust authentication and a world-accessible Unix domain socket in /tmp, allowing any local user on the same host to authenticate as the passwordless postgres superuser and execute arbitrary operating system commands as the msfdb owner. 


This issue is fixed in version 6.5.10.

cna.title: temporal-proxy can send decrypted failure messages and stack traces to the upstream in plaintext

descriptions.value: Disclosure of failure messages and stack traces, which the deployment encrypts to keep them from the upstream Temporal service, to anyone who can read Workflow history there. Payloads remain encrypted. Failure text the upstream has already stored in plaintext stays readable after upgrading, until the namespace's retention period expires. No integrity or availability impact was identified.

solutions.value: Upgrade to temporal-proxy 1.0.2, 1.1.2, or 1.2.1, as appropriate for the deployed minor release line. Fixed releases replace the message and clear the stack trace of every outbound failure that carries encoded attributes, in any encoding, whenever the proxy is configured with encryption keys, whether or not encryption.failures is set. A custom failure converter that sends readable text beside its own encoded attributes will find that text replaced at the upstream. Upgrading does not re-encrypt failure text the upstream already stores. Releases before 1.0.0 receive no fix.

descriptions.value: When payload encryption is enabled, failure messages and stack traces that temporal-proxy is configured to keep from the upstream Temporal service can reach it in plaintext, where anyone who can read the Workflow's history at the upstream can read them. When the proxy returns a failure to a Worker, it decrypts the failure's encoded attributes and copies the message and stack trace back onto the failure, keeping the attributes. A Worker that sends that failure back through the proxy, as SDKs do when an Activity failure becomes the cause of a Workflow failure, sends the restored text with it, and the proxy forwards the text unchanged because the failure already has encoded attributes. The upstream then stores the text in plaintext beside its encrypted copy. This affects deployments that enable failure encryption in the proxy, and deployments that leave it off while the SDK encodes failure attributes itself. Payloads are not affected. temporal-proxy versions 0.9.0 through 1.2.0 are affected. The issue is fixed in 1.0.2, 1.1.2, and 1.2.1, and releases before 1.0.0 receive no fix. Upgrade to the fixed release for the deployed minor release line.

@fastify/middie is the middleware engine that adds Express and Connect style middleware support to Fastify. In versions 8.3.0 through 9.3.6, the internal helper that normalizes a path-scoped middleware's mount path only handles string inputs, but the use method also accepts an array of mount paths and passes it through unchanged, so the normalization silently does nothing. As a result, a trailing slash on an array element survives into the generated route-matching regular expression, and an element that is exactly the root path, meaning a catch-all mount, is dropped entirely. Requests to subroutes of the affected mount paths then skip the path-scoped middleware, such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting, while Fastify's router still dispatches them to the handler, allowing an unauthenticated client to reach protected routes. Applications are affected when they mount middleware on an array of paths in which an element ends with a slash, including one introduced by a plugin prefix that ends with a slash, or is exactly the root path. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.7, and users should upgrade to 9.3.7 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, and avoid array mount paths with a trailing slash element for security relevant middleware.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), the row-level security policies on pem.job and pem.jobstep that apply to PEM agents do not limit an agent to its own jobs. An attacker who controls one monitored host, and so its PEM agent certificate, can create, change or delete jobs for every other agent, including the agent on the PEM server. Agents run SQL job steps with the database credentials of the server they monitor, and shell job steps where batch jobs are enabled, so compromising one monitored host can give superuser SQL access to every monitored database and to the PEM backend.
From PEM 10.6.1, PEM agents can no longer create jobs or change job definitions or job steps.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Delegation requests only name sharing groups

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Delegation requests only name sharing groups
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix adds an authorization check using checkIfAuthorised() on the submitted sharing_group_id before it is persisted. The ID is validated as a positive integer (ctype_digit) and the requesting user's membership in the referenced sharing group is verified. If the ID is malformed, missing, or the user is not a member, a generic 404 NotFoundException is raised, producing the same response for all unauthorized or invalid inputs to prevent enumeration. The validated (or default '0') value is then stored, ensuring only authorized sharing group references are recorded.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; the fix applies to the codebase at the time of the commit and all prior versions lacking the checkIfAuthorised call in delegateEvent.
PR:L assumes the attacker needs a standard authenticated user with perm_delegate; the exact role requirements are inferred from the test setup (least_privileged_role with perm_add and perm_delegate).
VC:L assumes the sharing group name is the only sensitive data disclosed; the patch does not indicate that group membership lists or other metadata are leaked.
CAPEC-126 (Parameter Tampering) is the closest available mapping; a dedicated IDOR or broken-object-level-authorization CAPEC is not present in the catalog.
The Co-Authored-By line credits an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) as a remediation developer; this is recorded as it appears in the commit metadata but is atypical for CVE credit conventions.
The commit date (2026-11-09) is taken at face value from the patch metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In EventDelegationsController.php delegateEvent(), a new block validates the submitted sharing_group_id: it casts the value to a string, checks ctype_digit, and calls SharingGroup::checkIfAuthorised() with the current user. On failure it throws NotFoundException. The previously inline ternary that stored the raw submitted value is replaced with the validated $sharingGroupId variable. A regression test class EventDelegationSharingGroupAcl is added to tests/testregressions.py covering: rejection of unauthorized, missing, and malformed sharing group IDs with uniform 404 responses; acceptance of the requester's own sharing group with distribution 4; ignoring of sharing_group_id when distribution is not 4; and confirmation that a site admin may reference any sharing group.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a web application accessed over the network. AC:L: The attack requires only submitting a different sharing_group_id value in a standard HTTP POST; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N: No attack target manipulation is needed. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated user with delegation permission (perm_delegate). UI:N: No victim interaction is required beyond the attacker's own request. VC:L: The impact is limited to disclosure of a sharing group's name (a short string), not full data or credentials. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: No impact on subsequent components.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-126 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: The fix adds an authorization check using checkIfAuthorised() on the submitted sharing_group_id before it is persisted. The ID is validated as a positive integer (ctype_digit) and the requesting user's membership in the referenced sharing group is verified. If the ID is malformed, missing, or the user is not a member, a generic 404 NotFoundException is raised, producing the same response for all unauthorized or invalid inputs to prevent enumeration. The validated (or default '0') value is then stored, ensuring only authorized sharing group references are recorded.

descriptions.value: MISP's EventDelegationsController delegateEvent method accepted a user-supplied sharing_group_id parameter without verifying that the requesting user was a member of the referenced sharing group. When a delegation request was submitted with distribution set to 4 (sharing-group distribution), the raw sharing_group_id value was stored directly into the EventDelegation record. The delegation view subsequently rendered the stored sharing group's name back to the requester. Because no authorization check was performed, any authenticated user with delegation permission could enumerate sharing group identifiers (by guessing sequential IDs or other values) and read the names of sharing groups to which their organisation did not belong, including hidden or restricted groups. Hidden, missing, and malformed identifiers were not distinguished in the response, but the successful case still leaked the group name. The vulnerability required an authenticated session with the perm_delegate capability and knowledge of a valid event ID to delegate. The security impact is limited to disclosure of sharing group names (a low-impact confidentiality breach) and does not grant access to the group's contents or modify any data.

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Login e-mails are admin-only under external
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The authorization check for changing a login email now explicitly denies the operation for non-site-admin users when any external authentication backend is active (Security.auth is set, ApacheSecureAuth.apacheEnv is configured, or Plugin.CustomAuth_enable is true). Only site administrators retain the ability to modify login emails in an external-authentication deployment, preventing non-admin users from redirecting their directory identity lookup to an arbitrary account.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; all versions prior to this commit that lack the external-auth check in __canChangeLogin() are assumed affected.

The vulnerability requires that at least one external authentication backend (Security.auth, ApacheSecureAuth, or CustomAuth) is configured; instances using only local MISP authentication are not affected by this specific issue.
The CVSS VC:L assumes the attacker gains data access scoped to the captured identity's permissions; a higher-privilege target could yield higher confidentiality impact.
CAPEC-126 (Privilege Escalation) is the closest standard mapping; no CAPEC specifically covers directory-identity capture via email-key substitution.

The SSVC technical_impact of 'total' assumes the captured directory identity's full privilege set is transferred to the attacker; if the target identity has limited privileges, the practical impact may be lower.
The commit date (2026-11-18) and AI co-authorship (Claude Opus 5.5) are noted from metadata but do not affect the vulnerability analysis.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Controller/UsersController.php, the __canChangeLogin() method was restructured: after the existing site-admin bypass and MISP.disable_user_login_change check, three additional conditions are now required for non-admins to change their login email: Security.auth must be empty, ApacheSecureAuth.apacheEnv must be unset, and Plugin.CustomAuth_enable must be unset. A new regression test class LoginChangeExternalAuth in tests/testregressions.py verifies that self-service and org-admin email changes are refused when external auth is enabled, while site-admin changes remain permitted, and that self-service changes still work when no external auth is configured.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L: The attack is a single API call to change the email field; no race conditions or special timing are needed. AT:N: No prior tampering of system data is required. PR:L: An authenticated non-admin user with a valid API key is sufficient. UI:N: No victim interaction is needed; the attacker acts on their own account. VC:L: The attacker gains read access to data visible to the captured identity. VI:H: The integrity of the identity-to-account binding is fundamentally broken; the attacker assumes a different identity and its privileges. VA:N: No denial-of-service impact. SC:N: No secondary-component confidentiality impact beyond what is captured. SI:H: The external directory's identity resolution is subverted for the attacker's session. SA:N: No availability impact on the directory service.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker, holding a low-privilege MISP account, changes their login email to match a higher-privilege directory account. On next login the external backend resolves the email to the target identity, granting the attacker the target's organization and role. This is a direct privilege escalation via identity capture. The mapping is the closest standard CAPEC; no more specific CAPEC for directory-identity capture exists in the CAPEC catalog.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The __canChangeLogin() authorization check failed to restrict the login-email change action based on the active authentication context. When external authentication was in use, the check should have denied non-admin email changes because the email is the directory identity key, but it only evaluated a single configuration flag.

The login email is a user-controlled key used by the external directory to resolve identity. Because non-admins could modify this key, they could redirect the directory lookup to an arbitrary account, bypassing the intended identity binding.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-126 Privilege Escalation

solutions.value: The authorization check for changing a login email now explicitly denies the operation for non-site-admin users when any external authentication backend is active (Security.auth is set, ApacheSecureAuth.apacheEnv is configured, or Plugin.CustomAuth_enable is true). Only site administrators retain the ability to modify login emails in an external-authentication deployment, preventing non-admin users from redirecting their directory identity lookup to an arbitrary account.

descriptions.value: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the user login-email change logic. When an external authentication backend is configured (LDAP, Shibboleth, ApacheSecureAuth, or CustomAuth), the login email address serves as the key by which the directory service resolves a user's identity, organization, and role on each login. The __canChangeLogin() method in UsersController only checked the MISP.disable_user_login_change setting and site-admin status; it did not account for whether an external authentication backend was active. As a result, any authenticated non-admin user (including org admins) could change their own login email to an address that matches a higher-privilege account in the external directory. On the user's next login, the external backend would resolve that email to the target directory identity, granting the attacker the organization and role associated with that identity. This constitutes an account-identity capture and privilege escalation: the attacker effectively assumes the identity of any directory account whose email they can guess or discover. The vulnerability requires an authenticated session with a valid API key or session token and a MISP instance configured with at least one external authentication backend. The impact is limited to the scope of the captured directory identity's privileges within MISP.

When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured to use TLS 1.3 early data using the ssl_early_data on directive, an attacker can use a specially crafted TLS 1.3 connection to drive an NGINX worker into a tight loop in which it repeatedly retries the same send without ever making progress. The worker continues accepting new connections and handling existing ones, but one CPU core is pinned at 100%.

Impact:
System performance can degrade until the NGINX worker process is either forced to restart or is manually restarted. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a degradation of service that can lead to a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Event searches match only what the user can
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces a visibleElementConditions() helper in the Event model that wraps every attribute- and object-level search subquery with the same distribution, sharing-group, and soft-deleted visibility rules enforced by MispAttribute::buildConditions(). New helper methods (visibleAttributeTagSubquery, visibleAttributeTagEventIds, visibleAttributeTagConditions) apply the same checks to tag-based filters. All search code paths in EventsController, Event, MispAttribute, MispObject, and ReportFromEvent now pass the authenticated user into these helpers so that sub-entities hidden from the user no longer influence search results.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; the fix is assumed to apply to all versions prior to this commit.
CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker needs a standard authenticated MISP account with access to at least one event; no specific role or permission beyond event visibility is required.

CVSS VC:L reflects that the disclosure is scoped to sub-entities within events the attacker can already see, not a full database dump; however, prefix enumeration can reconstruct full attribute values over time.
CAPEC-126 is the closest available mapping; no CAPEC precisely describes a search endpoint missing sub-entity authorization checks.
The commit date (2026-11-08) and the presence of 'Claude Opus 5.5' as co-author are taken at face value from the patch metadata; no independent verification was performed.
SSVC exploitation is set to 'none' because no PoC, active exploitation, or public disclosure is evidenced in the patch; the ENISA report is referenced but its contents are not available.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Added Event::visibleElementConditions(), Event::visibleAttributeTagSubquery(), Event::visibleAttributeTagEventIds(), Event::visibleAttributeTagConditions(), and Event::elementDistributionRules() to enforce per-attribute/object ACL and deleted-scope checks inside search subqueries. Modified EventsController __quickFilter, __setIndexFilterConditions, and __eventIdsTaggedWithGalaxy to use the new visibility-aware tag lookups instead of raw AttributeTag queries. Wrapped all attribute and object subquery conditions in set_filter_wildcard, set_filter_value, set_filter_uuid, add_value_filter_subquery, and MispObject::buildFilterConditions with visibleElementConditions(). Updated MispAttribute::set_filter_tags and ReportFromEvent::getObjects to pass the user context. Added a comprehensive regression test class EventSearchAttributeAcl covering value, prefix, searchall, tag, soft-deleted, object, galaxy, and quick-filter probes for an outsider, owner, and site admin.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L: The attack requires only standard search API calls with crafted values or prefixes; no race conditions or special timing. AT:N: No prior tampering with system data is needed. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated MISP user with access to at least one event that contains hidden sub-entities. UI:N: No victim interaction is required; the attacker queries their own search. VC:L: Confidentiality impact is limited to specific attribute values, tags, and existence of soft-deleted elements within events the attacker can already see; full system data is not exposed. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: No impact on other systems.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker leverages a legitimate trusted relationship (visibility of a community-distributed event) to probe sub-entities (attributes, objects, tags) that carry stricter access controls. The search API is a trusted, authenticated interface, but the sub-entity ACL was not enforced within it. This is the closest CAPEC to the pattern of using a permitted operation to access data at a finer granularity than the operation's authorization scope covers. Uncertainty: no CAPEC precisely models 'search endpoint missing sub-entity ACL'; CAPEC-126 is the best available match because the core mechanism is exploiting a broader trust (event visibility) to reach narrower-protected data (attribute values).

weaknessRationale.rationale: The search subqueries on attributes and objects lacked the per-element authorization checks (distribution, sharing group, soft-deleted scope) that are enforced elsewhere in MISP. The event-level ACL was satisfied, but the sub-entity-level ACL was absent from the search path.

The missing sub-entity authorization allowed an authenticated user to infer the existence and content (via prefix enumeration) of attributes, objects, and tags that were restricted to other organisations or sharing groups, or that had been soft-deleted.

solutions.value: The fix introduces a visibleElementConditions() helper in the Event model that wraps every attribute- and object-level search subquery with the same distribution, sharing-group, and soft-deleted visibility rules enforced by MispAttribute::buildConditions(). New helper methods (visibleAttributeTagSubquery, visibleAttributeTagEventIds, visibleAttributeTagConditions) apply the same checks to tag-based filters. All search code paths in EventsController, Event, MispAttribute, MispObject, and ReportFromEvent now pass the authenticated user into these helpers so that sub-entities hidden from the user no longer influence search results.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an authorization bypass in its event search and filter functionality. When a user performed searches through events/restSearch (value, value prefix, searchall, type, uuid, attribute tags, object filters), objects/restSearch, or the event index tag, galaxy, and quick filters, the underlying SQL subqueries matched against attributes and objects without enforcing the per-attribute distribution, sharing-group, or soft-deleted visibility rules that apply when fetching individual elements.

A user who could view an event (for example, a community-distributed event) could therefore use search to determine whether organisation-only, sharing-group-restricted, or soft-deleted attributes and objects existed within that event. Because the value filter supports prefix matching (LIKE), an attacker could enumerate the full value of a hidden attribute one character at a time. Tags attached exclusively to hidden attributes also leaked through the tag, galaxy, and quick-filter paths on the event index.

The vulnerability affects the EventsController quick-filter and index-filter logic, the Event model wildcard/value/uuid/tag filter methods, the MispAttribute tag filter, the MispObject buildFilterConditions and restSearch methods, and the ReportFromEvent object filter. Site administrators and users belonging to the event's own organisation retain full visibility, and sync users continue to match soft-deleted elements as intended.

The issue was reported by ENISA.

cna.title: Cyrus-sasl: scram channel-binding null dereference allows remote denial of service

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank YangHailong (Alipay Security Team) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
If SCRAM authentication is not required, remove the optional SCRAM plugin package to prevent the mechanism from being loaded:

# dnf remove cyrus-sasl-scram

Restart any services using Cyrus SASL to unload the plugin from memory:

# systemctl restart <service_name>

Alternatively, restrict network access to affected services to trusted IP addresses or subnets using firewalld:

# firewall-cmd --zone=trusted --add-source=<trusted_ip_or_subnet> --permanent
# firewall-cmd --reload

Caveats:
Removing cyrus-sasl-scram disables SCRAM authentication (SCRAM-SHA-1, SCRAM-SHA-256). Clients that only support SCRAM mechanisms will be unable to authenticate until alternative mechanisms (such as GSSAPI or PLAIN over TLS) are configured.

Warning: Restarting dependent services will temporarily terminate active client connections and disrupt availability during the restart window.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in cyrus-sasl. When processing authentication requests using the Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM), a remote attacker can trigger a null pointer dereference by submitting unexpected channel-binding data. This causes the server process to crash before validating authentication proofs, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS).

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Galaxy imports no longer rewrite default or
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces an object-level authorization check (__mayUpdateCapturedGalaxy) that enforces three rules before any existing galaxy record is modified: default galaxies are never updatable via import or sync; non-default galaxies may only be updated by a site admin, the owning organization, or a sync user who has visibility on the record. The role-level permission check is moved before the captureOrganisationAndSG() call so that no organization or sharing-group data is captured for an unauthorized user. When an update is permitted, the org_id, orgc_id, and default fields are explicitly excluded from the write, preventing ownership transfer or default-flag demotion even by authorized updaters.
assumptions: The affected MISP version range is not specified in the patch; the vulnerability is assumed to affect all versions containing the vulnerable captureGalaxy() logic prior to this commit.
The perm_galaxy_editor role is assumed to be a low-privilege role available to non-admin users; if it is restricted to admins only, the PR metric would be H rather than L.

The CAPEC-114 mapping is the closest available pattern; no CAPEC specifically covers 'authorization bypass via object-level key matching in a CRUD operation', so Parameter Tampering is used as the best approximation.
The CVSS VA:L rating assumes that demoting default galaxies degrades but does not fully break instance functionality; if default galaxies are critical for core operations, VA could be H.

The SSVC technical_impact of 'partial' assumes the integrity compromise does not cascade into a full loss of trust in the MISP instance's data; if downstream consumers rely on galaxy ownership for access control, the impact could be 'total'.

The patch does not specify whether the vulnerability is exploitable via the sync/pull path ($fromPull=true) in addition to the manual import path; both paths share the same captureGalaxy() code and are assumed equally affected.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Galaxy.php: (1) a new private method __mayUpdateCapturedGalaxy() is added, returning false for default galaxies, true for site admins or same-org users, and true for sync users only if the galaxy passes the user's visibility conditions; (2) the existing-galaxy lookup and the __mayUpdateCapturedGalaxy() gate are moved before the captureOrganisationAndSG() call, so unauthorized users are rejected before any org/SG capture; (3) the role permission check (perm_site_admin / perm_galaxy_editor) is moved to the top of the method, before any data mutation; (4) when an existing galaxy is updated, org_id, orgc_id, and default are unset from the existing record before the field-diff loop, ensuring they are never overwritten; (5) a regression test suite (GalaxyCaptureUpdateGate in tests/testregressions.py) is added covering: other-org editor cannot update visible or hidden galaxies, owner can update own galaxy, sync user can update visible but not hidden galaxies, site admin can update without taking over, a
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L: The attacker only needs to submit a valid import payload with a matching UUID; no race conditions or special timing are required. AT:N: No attack-target manipulation is needed. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated user with the perm_galaxy_editor role (a low-privilege role in MISP). UI:N: No victim interaction is required; the import is a server-side operation. VC:N: No confidentiality impact is evident from the patch. VI:H: Integrity of galaxy records is severely compromised: ownership (org_id, orgc_id) is transferred and the default flag is cleared, corrupting shared threat-intelligence metadata. VA:L: Demoting default galaxies may degrade the instance's threat-intelligence functionality for all users, but the service remains operational. SC:N: No secondary confidentiality impact. SI:H: Secondary integrity impact extends to other organizations' galaxy data and the shared default galaxy set. SA:N: No secondary availability impact beyond the primary VA.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker crafts a galaxy import payload whose UUID field is set to match an existing galaxy (default or another organization's), thereby targeting a specific record for unauthorized modification. The UUID is a user-controlled parameter that the application used to identify the target object without sufficient authorization validation. This is the closest CAPEC pattern: the attacker tampers with a request parameter (UUID) to redirect the application's write operation to an unintended object. Uncertainty: CAPEC-114 is a broad pattern; a more specific 'authorization bypass' CAPEC does not exist in the catalog, so this is the best available match.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The captureGalaxy() method performed only a coarse role-level check (perm_galaxy_editor) without verifying object-level ownership or the default-galaxy status of the target record. Any user with the editor role could overwrite galaxies belonging to other organizations or system default galaxies, which is a missing object-level authorization control.

The attacker-supplied UUID in the import payload was used as the sole key to locate and overwrite an existing galaxy record. Because no ownership or default-status check was applied to the matched record, a user-controlled key (UUID) effectively bypassed the intended authorization boundary. This is a secondary, more specific manifestation of the missing authorization.

events.description: Corrective change authored (fc1ce99a660b6f34e936b1947167de6748c11ecd): fix: [security] Galaxy imports no longer rewrite default or
Patch retrieved from the supplied URL; retrieval time is used as the default availability time.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-114 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: The fix introduces an object-level authorization check (__mayUpdateCapturedGalaxy) that enforces three rules before any existing galaxy record is modified: default galaxies are never updatable via import or sync; non-default galaxies may only be updated by a site admin, the owning organization, or a sync user who has visibility on the record. The role-level permission check is moved before the captureOrganisationAndSG() call so that no organization or sharing-group data is captured for an unauthorized user. When an update is permitted, the org_id, orgc_id, and default fields are explicitly excluded from the write, preventing ownership transfer or default-flag demotion even by authorized updaters.

descriptions.value: MISP contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the Galaxy import/sync functionality (captureGalaxy in app/Model/Galaxy.php). The captureGalaxy() method matched an incoming galaxy payload to an existing galaxy by UUID and unconditionally overwrote the matched record, regardless of whether the importing user belonged to the owning organization or whether the galaxy was a system-provided default galaxy. Any authenticated user holding the perm_galaxy_editor role could therefore: (1) demote a default galaxy by setting its default flag to false, (2) reassign the galaxy's org_id and orgc_id to the attacker's organization, effectively taking ownership, and (3) modify other galaxy fields (name, description, distribution, version). Additionally, the role-level permission check (perm_site_admin or perm_galaxy_editor) was executed after the captureOrganisationAndSG() call, meaning organization and sharing-group data was already captured before the authorization decision was made. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with the perm_galaxy_editor role and the ability to submit a galaxy import payload containing a UUID that matches an existing galaxy. The security impact is loss of data integrity across the MISP instance: default galaxy definitions are corrupted, cross-organization ownership is silently transferred, and the integrity of shared threat-intelligence galaxy metadata is compromised for all users of the instance.

cna.title: Inscriptis: Quadratic memory growth from sibling <table> elements in get_text()

descriptions.value: Inscriptis is a Python library for converting HTML to text. From 2.0.0 until 2.7.6, when the parent is block-level, table_end_handler() in model/tag/table_tag.py writes each sibling table through HtmlElement.write_verbatim_text() in model/html_element.py; Canvas.open_block() leaves the parent padding_inline prefix on the stack, Canvas.close_block() does not remove it, and only Canvas.close_tag() calls prefix.remove_last_prefix(). Each following sibling table therefore carries forward accumulated indentation, making get_text() output grow quadratically and allowing small attacker-controlled HTML to exhaust memory in applications converting it without authentication or user interaction. This issue is fixed in 2.7.6.

cna.title: Apache Iggy Go SDK: Go TCP client creates personal access tokens that outlive the requested expiry

descriptions.value:
Insufficient Session Expiration vulnerability in the Apache Iggy Go SDK. The TCP client method CreatePersonalAccessToken wrote the 32-bit expiry into the upper half of the 64-bit expiry field that the server reads. The server read a nonzero expiry as 2^32 times the requested value. A token created through the Go TCP client therefore stayed valid about four billion times longer than the caller asked for.

This issue affects Apache Iggy Go SDK: from 0.5.0 before 0.10.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.10.0, which fixes the issue. Tokens that an earlier version created keep their long expiry on the server. Delete those tokens and create new ones.

cna.title: svglib: Exponential resource consumption via nested <use> references in svg2rlg

descriptions.description: CWE-776: Improper Restriction of Recursive Entity References in DTDs

descriptions.value: svglib reads SVG files and converts them to other formats. Prior to 2.3.1, the svg2rlg() renderer recursively expands nested SVG <use> references by deep-copying each referenced subtree; SvgRenderer.renderUse() in src/svglib/svglib.py calls xlink_href_target(), which rejects direct cycles but permits acyclic reference graphs with repeated fan-out. A small attacker-controlled SVG can therefore trigger exponentially increasing node expansion, consuming excessive CPU and memory in any application that renders it without a non-default option; HTML-to-PDF workflows using xhtml2pdf can reach the same renderer when an embedded data:image/svg+xml image in an HTML img element is passed to pisa.CreatePDF(). This issue is fixed in 2.3.1.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Anonymised sightings cannot be attributed

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Anonymised sightings cannot be attributed
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: A new authorization check (orgFilterAllowed) is introduced in the Sighting model. When Sightings_anonymise is enabled, a non-site-admin user's org_id filter targeting another organisation is rejected: listSightings returns an empty result set, and restSearch either skips the negated condition or substitutes an impossible value (-1) for the positive filter. Site administrators and users filtering by their own organisation retain full functionality. When anonymization is disabled, the filter behaves as before.
assumptions: The Sightings_anonymise setting must be enabled for the vulnerability to be exploitable; when disabled, the org_id filter is expected behavior and not a vulnerability.
The user must have perm_sighting (sighting read permission) but must NOT be a site admin (perm_site_admin); site admins are explicitly allowed to filter by any organisation.

The affected version range is unknown; the patch does not specify a version boundary. All versions of MISP with the Sightings_anonymise feature and the pre-fix listSightings/restSearch code are assumed affected.
CAPEC-66 (Parameter Tampering) is the closest available attack pattern; no CAPEC specifically describes bypassing an anonymization control via a filter parameter, so this mapping carries uncertainty.

CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker needs only a standard authenticated MISP user account with sighting read permissions; the exact minimum role is inferred from the test setup (least_privileged_role with perm_add and perm_sighting).
The Co-Authored-By line references an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5); it is credited as a tool rather than a human remediation developer.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: Adds a private method orgFilterAllowed() to app/Model/Sighting.php that returns true only when anonymization is off, the user is a site admin, or the org_id matches the user's own organisation. In listSightings(), an early return of an empty array is inserted when the filter is not allowed. In restSearch(), when the filter is not allowed, negated conditions are skipped (continue) and positive conditions are set to org_id = -1 to match nothing. A new regression test class SightingsAnonymisedOrgFilter in tests/testregressions.py validates that non-admins cannot unmask reporters via either endpoint, that site admins retain filter access, and that the filter remains functional when anonymization is disabled.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application; the vulnerable endpoints are HTTP APIs. AC:L: Exploitation requires only adding an org_id parameter to a standard API call; no race conditions, timing, or complex setup needed. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L: An authenticated user with perm_sighting (sighting read) is sufficient; site admin is not required. UI:N: No victim interaction is needed; the attacker simply calls the API. VC:L: The impact is limited to revealing which organisation reported a sighting; full record contents and other data remain protected. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: No impact on subsequent components or safety.

capecRationale.rationale: The attacker manipulates the org_id request parameter to filter results by a specific organisation, thereby bypassing the anonymization control. This is the closest CAPEC to the observed attack: a legitimate parameter is used in a way that circumvents a security policy (anonymization). Uncertainty: this is not a classic parameter tampering (e.g., altering a price or ID to access another user's data) but rather exploiting a filter parameter to infer information that should be masked. No CAPEC specifically covers 'bypassing anonymization via filter parameter', so CAPEC-66 is the best available match.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The primary impact is disclosure of the reporter's organisation identity, which the anonymization feature is designed to conceal. A non-privileged user can determine which organisation reported a sighting by filtering on that organisation's ID.

The root cause is the absence of an authorization check on the org_id filter parameter. The endpoint accepted and applied any caller-supplied organisation ID without verifying whether the requesting user was permitted to filter by that organisation, especially in the context of anonymized sightings.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-66 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: A new authorization check (orgFilterAllowed) is introduced in the Sighting model. When Sightings_anonymise is enabled, a non-site-admin user's org_id filter targeting another organisation is rejected: listSightings returns an empty result set, and restSearch either skips the negated condition or substitutes an impossible value (-1) for the positive filter. Site administrators and users filtering by their own organisation retain full functionality. When anonymization is disabled, the filter behaves as before.

descriptions.value: MISP contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the Sighting model when the Sightings_anonymise setting is enabled. The listSightings and sightings/restSearch endpoints accepted a caller-supplied org_id filter parameter and applied it directly to the SQL query without verifying whether the requesting user was authorized to filter by that organisation. Because the anonymization mechanism masks the reporter's organisation in the returned records, a non-site-admin user could bypass the anonymization by specifying another organisation's ID in the filter. The query would then return only that organisation's sightings, effectively naming the reporter and defeating the purpose of the anonymization feature. A negated filter (NOT IN) similarly revealed which sightings belonged to the target organisation by exclusion. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with sighting read permissions (perm_sighting) who is not a site administrator, and the Sightings_anonymise plugin setting must be enabled. The security impact is the disclosure of which organisation reported a given sighting, undermining the privacy guarantees that the anonymization feature is designed to provide. This issue was reported by ENISA.
